decisions.question: Writers before readers: how does start() settle a writer's first emission before a reader connects (Spec §3.13 step 1: 'each topology's first emission sees inputs that their writers have already settled')?

options.label: Synchronously within start(), from the bus's own queue
options.consequence: start() connects each bootstrap activation in the connection order and, before the next connects, delivers the publishes its connection causes and those their deliveries cause; start() still delivers the queue before it returns, as v1's G34 did, so consumer tests that assert right after start() keep working; a self-reference that never settles keeps start() from returning, as it would keep the reentrant drain from ending after start().

options.label: Sequence the connections through provider-zone microtasks
options.consequence: Each next connection waits for the zone's microtasks; the bus cannot drain the zone's queue in production, a microtask a delivery schedules lands after the next connection, and the queue is delivered after start() returns, which every consumer suite that asserts right after start() would notice.

options.label: Connect every activation, then deliver the connections' publishes
options.consequence: What the minimal barrier of topology-dsl-write-chain does: a reader activated before its writer first sees its input's initial value, then the settled one (probe P2: y=0 then y=20), the flicker Guide §6.1 describes and Spec §3.13 forbids.

decisions.chosen: Synchronously within start(), from the bus's own queue
decisions.why: It is the only option that meets Spec §3.13 step 1 exactly while keeping 'start() delivers the queue before it returns'. The publishes a connection causes are the bus's own (they pass through its publish path), so the bus can deliver them without touching the zone's microtask queue, on the production provider as on a TestBus. 'Settled' covers what a writer emits synchronously from its reads' first values; a value it emits from a timer or asynchronous work reaches readers later, which G34 states. Measured: probe P2 and the G34 settled-writer case pass only on the v2 runtime; the seeded defect that defers the connection's publishes to a microtask fails four G34 cases.
evidence: hsdd/contract/fixture/bus-api/behavior/bus_api_conformance.dart G34 'start connects a writer before every topology...'

decisions.question: When, and in what order relative to the bootstrap topologies, does start() connect the observed subscriptions made during bootstrap, and when do they receive their first values (ADR-003 item 6 as amended: 'within start() or in provider-zone work that start() schedules')?

options.label: After every topology, first values within start()
options.consequence: A state subscriber's first value is the settled one; it receives its first values and then the queue before start() returns, in order; an event a writer publishes while start() connects it reaches no bootstrap subscription, as it reaches no reader connected after it.

options.label: After every topology, first values in the first provider-zone microtask after start()
options.consequence: Mirrors G17's microtask, with the queue buffered behind the replay; tests must flush after start() to see a bootstrap subscriber's values, and the queue reaches topologies and subscriptions at different moments.

options.label: Before the topologies
options.consequence: Event subscribers also see what writers publish while connecting, but a state subscriber first sees the initial value and then the settled one, the order dependence Spec §3.13 removes.

decisions.chosen: After every topology, first values within start()
decisions.why: A subscription is a reader of its topic, so it connects after the writers, as Spec §3.13 orders topologies; Spec §2.1 'Replay timing' has the bus control when a subscriber receives its first value where the barrier depends on it, so start() delivers it itself. ADR-003 item 6 leaves the timing here. Spec §3.13 step 1 says the bus 'also connects' the subscriptions without ordering them against the topologies, so the order is marked for upstreaming. Signal that would have changed my mind: a consumer fixture that expects a bootstrap subscriber to receive an event a topology publishes while connecting; none does (every other suite replays as before on the v2 runtime but for scope timing and the error zone).
evidence: docs/auto-run/experiments/bus-api-v2/output.txt T6, T9, T10 (defect: subscriptions connected before the topologies)

decisions.question: Is the connection order computed by the bus, or does this handoff ask topology-ir@v1 for a new analysis function (the intake allows a compatible one)?

options.label: The bus computes it from the definitions' reads and writes
options.consequence: No contract changes outside bus-api; the order is stated in the delivery rules (the earliest activated of the activations not yet connected that reads no topic another of them writes).

options.label: Request a topology-ir@v1 analysis function
options.consequence: Tooling could print the order, but a request entry and a topology-ir handoff for a computation only the runtime uses.

decisions.chosen: The bus computes it from the definitions' reads and writes
decisions.why: Only the runtime needs the order, every definition it needs is already in hand at activation, and the rule fits in one sentence. No evidence beyond that; the signal that would change it is a tool (graph renderer, lint) that must show the bootstrap order.

decisions.question: Scope timing (Spec §7.2): with what error does the bus reject a MODULE or PAGE activation, and a ModuleScope.acquire, before start() ('a diagnostic naming the topology', inside this contract)?

options.label: StateError naming the topology (and the module)
options.consequence: The Interface's misuse rule already names StateError for an operation the bus's state excludes; no sealed family grows; the message names the topology id and scope, or the module and its topologies; consumers that activate MODULE or PAGE topologies or acquire modules before start() break (bus-testing@v1 seven cases, flutter-binding@v1 two G8 cases).

options.label: A new BusError variant carrying the topology id and scope
options.consequence: A structured field, but adding a variant to the sealed BusError breaks every exhaustive switch (the surface set's included), for a programming error no consumer handles.

options.label: A topology-ir@v1 finding
options.consequence: Breaking under topology-ir@v1's closed finding family, and CI cannot see when an activation happens relative to start() (intake L2).

decisions.chosen: StateError naming the topology (and the module)
decisions.why: Lifecycle-state rejections are already StateError (shutdown), the rejection is a bootstrap-order mistake rather than a declaration finding, and the Spec's 'diagnostic naming the topology' is met by the message. The rejection itself is the Specification's; it removes a behavior consumer fixtures relied on (activating a MODULE or PAGE topology, or acquiring a module, before start()), so it is flagged as a breaking amend. Signal that would favor a variant: a consumer that must catch this rejection and branch on its fields.

decisions.question: Where does scope timing live among the guarantees: a new id, or folded into G22 and G34?

options.label: New G42 for the rejection; LateApplicationActivation stays in G22
options.consequence: Gates that restrict to existing ids keep selecting what they selected; the rejection cases are attributable to one id; H11 adds G42 to the restrictions it needs (provisionally delivered at nidana.runtime.14, whose replay is unrestricted).

options.label: Fold the rejection into G22 and G34
options.consequence: No new id, but G22 and G34 grow further and a gate restricted to G22 at nidana.runtime.12 would select the module-acquire case before modules exist.

decisions.chosen: New G42 for the rejection; LateApplicationActivation stays in G22
decisions.why: The prompt keeps ids where the meaning carries over; the rejection is a new meaning and the late-APPLICATION report is the old one. G42's acquire case needs module scopes, which nidana.runtime.14 delivers, hence that phase in the Delivery paragraph until H11 re-plans.

decisions.question: State what LateApplicationActivation reports (Spec §7.2: EventTopic events published before the activation were not delivered to it): a new field, or the existing one with its meaning stated?

options.label: Keep topologyId only; G22 and the doc comment state the meaning
options.consequence: No declaration change; the developer finds the topology's event reads from its id; a field naming them can come later as a new getter, which the Compatible list admits.

options.label: Add a field listing the event topics the topology reads
options.consequence: More precise console output, but a constructor change in a version whose declarations are otherwise unchanged, and every stand-in and surface library changes with it.

decisions.chosen: Keep topologyId only; G22 and the doc comment state the meaning
decisions.why: The Specification asks for a diagnostic that states the fact, which the type and its documented meaning do; v2 changes no declaration. The field is listed under 'Not in v2'. No evidence either way; the signal is a developer asking which topics were affected.

decisions.question: Subscriber errors (Spec §10.2 principle 5, §3.10): restate G5, G18 and G41's 'goes to the provider zone's uncaught-error handler' as amended ADR-003 decides.

options.label: Adopt ADR-003 as amended: callbacks in the provider zone, errors to the listen zone
options.consequence: G5 and G18 take S58's sentences; what a callback throws, and an error event left without onError, reach the uncaught-error handler of the zone in which listen was called; bus-testing@v1's G3 case, which expects a subscriber's error in the zone that built the scheduler, breaks until H4 restates G11.

options.label: Keep the provider zone
options.consequence: Contradicts Spec §10.2 principle 5 and ADR-003 item 2 as amended; a test whose subscriber throws passes while the error is reported elsewhere (subscriber-error-zone T2).

decisions.chosen: Adopt ADR-003 as amended: callbacks in the provider zone, errors to the listen zone
decisions.why: Decided by the Specification and by H1's amendment of ADR-003; the stand-in forwards exactly as docs/auto-run/experiments/subscriber-error-zone/ measured. It removes a behavior a consumer fixture relied on (bus-testing@v1's G3 case), hence the breaking-amend flag.

decisions.question: G41: an observed subscription that cannot convert a value to its type argument: S58's 'TypeError to the listen zone's handler, value skipped', or an error event as Dart's Stream.cast delivers it?

options.label: An error event in place of the value, as Stream.cast
options.consequence: onError receives the TypeError, or without one the listen zone's handler (G18's rule for an unhandled error event); the subscription keeps receiving unless it listened with cancelOnError; consistent with how TopicRemoved reaches a subscription.

options.label: Always to the listen zone's handler, value skipped
options.consequence: S58's proposed sentence; a subscriber with onError never sees the failure, unlike every other Dart stream that converts.

decisions.chosen: An error event in place of the value, as Stream.cast
decisions.why: A widened subscription is conceptually the subject's stream cast to the reference's type argument, and Dart's own cast delivers a failed cast as an error event (subscriber-error-zone C12, off-type-delivery case 2). It satisfies ADR-003 item 2 as amended either way: without onError the error reaches the listen zone. No consumer fixture publishes an off-type value; flutter-binding@v1's topic widgets observe at Object?, so no conversion of theirs can fail.

decisions.question: G41: what does 'an exception raised by the bus's own delivery code is an implementation defect and is not swallowed' (Spec §10.2 principle 5) mean for the conversion of an off-type value at a topology read (v1: skipped, TypeError to the provider zone's handler, nidana.runtime D5)?

options.label: A read-stage error: catchError recovers it, else it ends the write chains it reaches
options.consequence: The conversion belongs to the read it serves, as G41 already said; it flows downstream like any stage error, carrying the lineage the value would have had, so topology-dsl@v2's write-chain rule applies (PipelineTerminated in dev mode); no zone handler receives it; reverses nidana.runtime D5's skip.

options.label: The bus's own delivery code: not caught, propagates from the delivering call
options.consequence: A caller's misuse of a widened reference would surface as an exception out of publish or start() part way through a fan-out, breaking Spec §3.10's no-partial-fan-out rule.

options.label: A reported skip as in v1
options.consequence: The read skips the value and the error goes to the provider zone's handler: a special case no other stage has, and a provider-zone delivery of an error that Spec §10.2 principle 5 now routes nowhere.

decisions.chosen: A read-stage error: catchError recovers it, else it ends the write chains it reaches
decisions.why: Spec §10.2 principle 5 names three places an exception can be raised (transformer or operator, observer, shell subscriber); a read stage is part of the pipeline, so its failure is a stage error, and the 'own delivery code' sentence then means genuine runtime defects, which G13 now says the bus does not swallow. topology-dsl@v2's Errors and lineage left this choice to bus-api. It reverses a recorded node decision (nidana.runtime D5) and v1 amendment (g), so it is flagged; no consumer fixture relied on the skip.
evidence: docs/auto-run/experiments/bus-api-v2/output.txt T6, T10 (defect: a read that skips)

decisions.question: Where does this contract state the 'own delivery code' rule?

options.label: G13's last sentence, not executable
options.consequence: The bus catches only what an observer, a subscriber's callback or a pipeline stage raises; listed under Validation as not executable.

options.label: Leave it unstated
options.consequence: Spec §10.2 principle 5's sentence would have no home, and a runtime might wrap its delivery in a catch-all.

decisions.chosen: G13's last sentence, not executable
decisions.why: It is a rule implementers must follow even though no conformance case can make a correct runtime raise one; stating it keeps a catch-all out of the runtime.

decisions.question: Name check (Spec §4.3, §3.1): does tracing stay among G7's compared fields, which v0.15.1 lists without it; and how are 'the first use of each declaration' and the name freed by removeTopic stated?

options.label: Tracing stays, marked for upstreaming; every use compared; initial value not compared; removal frees the name
options.consequence: Behavior unchanged from v1 (compatible); observer gating keeps one tracing flag per subject; a new G7 case pins the initial-value and free-name clauses.

options.label: Drop tracing to match Spec §4.3
options.consequence: Two declarations differing only in tracing would share a subject whose gating follows whichever registered first, so an untraced declaration could be observed, or a traced one hidden.

decisions.chosen: Tracing stays, marked for upstreaming; every use compared; initial value not compared; removal frees the name
decisions.why: DEC-168's reason holds: observer gating (G30) reads one flag per subject. Comparing every use covers 'the first use of each declaration' and gives the same answer, since a declaration is a value. Decided with the L4 to L6 batch; logged without its own line, so this stamp is that batch's.
evidence: docs/auto-run/experiments/bus-api-v2/output.txt T6 (the new G7 case passes on the v1 runtime)

decisions.question: Re-activation (Spec §3.9; Guide §6.3 'Name every transformer'): IR equality as in v1 (DEC-167), or IR equality plus == on the plan's functions and seeds?

options.label: IR equality plus == on the plan's functions and seeds
options.consequence: A declaration differing in a scan seed or a closure body throws TopologyConflict; an inline closure or a tear-off on a receiver declare creates is unequal to its own next evaluation, so such a topology cannot be activated twice while active; flutter-binding@v1 Refinement 4's holder counts work only for page topologies with named functions (its fixtures' page topology has none, so they pass); navigation-api's resolver, whose stage functions are tear-offs on receivers its declare creates, conflicts with its own second activation.

options.label: IR equality as in v1
options.consequence: No false conflicts, but two different declarations under one id (another seed, another closure body) silently share the first activation, which Spec §3.9's 'any other observable difference' forbids.

decisions.chosen: IR equality plus == on the plan's functions and seeds
decisions.why: The Guide states the reason (re-activation compares transformers, a Dart closure equals only itself) and Spec §3.9 asks for a throw on any observable difference; the decision policy decides for the option with a stated reason. Probe P1 settles which functions compare equal: top-level and static tear-offs, tear-offs on one const receiver and const callable objects; not closures, not tear-offs on new receivers even with ==. Supersedes DEC-167.

decisions.question: Write chains (Spec §10.2, Appendix A.4): restate G26 and PipelineTerminated per write chain; how are the claims after a chain ends pinned?

options.label: Restate G26 in place, compatible, and pin claims kept with a new case
options.consequence: One report per chain the error ends (two for an error reaching two sinks); the error reaches no topic; a claim on an ended chain's state topic is rejected until deactivation; the v1 runtime passes the new case, so this change rides along.

options.label: Treat it as a new guarantee id
options.consequence: Gates restricted to G26 would miss the claims case; the meaning of G26 carries over.

decisions.chosen: Restate G26 in place, compatible, and pin claims kept with a new case
decisions.why: A sink and its write chain are one to one, so v1's per-sink report count equals v2's per-chain count; the upstream cancellation is topology-dsl@v2's and replays through bus_activation_test.dart (49 of 49 on the v2 runtime). S59 left the claims case to this contract.

decisions.question: During bootstrap, what does removeTopic do for a topic that an unconnected activation reads or an unconnected subscription observes?

options.label: Refuse without force; forced, end the subscription at once and give the read TopicRemoved when start() connects it
options.consequence: G9's v1 outcome (the chains that read the topic end, the subscription ends) holds before start() too; a new G9 case pins it.

options.label: Let the unconnected read reconnect to the fresh subject at start()
options.consequence: A forced removal would silently not affect a bootstrap topology, unlike the same removal after start().

decisions.chosen: Refuse without force; forced, end the subscription at once and give the read TopicRemoved when start() connects it
decisions.why: Keeps G9 meaning the same thing whenever it is called. No Specification text covers the case; the seeded defect that lets the read reconnect fails the new case.

decisions.question: What becomes of an activation deactivated before start()?

options.label: Never connected; claims released at once (G25)
options.consequence: Deactivation means the same before start() as after; a new G25 case pins it.

options.label: Connected at start() anyway
options.consequence: A topology the bootstrap withdrew would compute once.

decisions.chosen: Never connected; claims released at once (G25)
decisions.why: Follows from 'start() connects the activations still active'; no evidence needed beyond the case.

decisions.question: Does scope timing (Spec §7.2) also reject a shell publisher bound to a MODULE or PAGE scope before start()?

options.label: No: a publisher of any scope works before start()
options.consequence: G42 states it; flutter-binding's PageScope publishers are created at mount, after start() in a conforming app.

options.label: Reject it too
options.consequence: A rule the Specification does not state, breaking publisher construction during bootstrap for no stated hazard.

decisions.chosen: No: a publisher of any scope works before start()
decisions.why: Spec §7.2's timing rule names activations; a publisher's scope only bounds its claims (Spec §7.2 scope compatibility). No evidence beyond the text.

decisions.question: The v1 suite activated MODULE topologies before start() in cases that test something else (limits, claims, conflicts, cycles, observers, telemetry, shutdown, the graph). How are they rewritten?

options.label: APPLICATION scope where the case is about bootstrap checks, start() first elsewhere
options.consequence: G10, G20, G21, G24's cycle case, G37 and G6 keep pinning that checks and claims are immediate during bootstrap; the rest start first and test what they tested.

options.label: Start first in every such case
options.consequence: Simpler, but nothing would pin that rejections stay immediate before start() (Spec §3.13 'validate and claim at once').

decisions.chosen: APPLICATION scope where the case is about bootstrap checks, start() first elsewhere
decisions.why: Spec §3.13 makes the bootstrap checks immediate; those cases are where that is pinned.

decisions.question: Check G8 and G35 against Spec §2.5's 'most recently delivered' and §3.13's 'measured on the bus's scheduler'.

options.label: Unchanged; G35 names the bus's scheduler
options.consequence: G8 already states the initial value until a publish is delivered, then the last delivered, and no queued publish; G35's timer is a provider-zone timer, the bus's scheduler (ADR-003 item 1); its text says so.

options.label: Restate G8 for the settled values start() delivers
options.consequence: Nothing to restate: values settled in start() step 1 are delivered values.

decisions.chosen: Unchanged; G35 names the bus's scheduler
decisions.why: Both already meet v0.15.1; the existing G8 and G35 cases pass on every runtime.

options.label: v2: barrier, scope timing, subscriber errors and conversions, and re-activation are breaking; write chains and the name check compatible
options.consequence: bus-api.md becomes v2 with a migration note per change; every live citation of bus-api@v1 elsewhere (contracts, ADR-003, specs, plan text) moves to v2 inside the intake; v1 keeps no file.

options.consequence: Contradicts the Breaking list (a delivery rule, the timing of first delivery, which operation throws what, and what happens to an off-type value, which v1 amendment (g) made breaking); the v1 runtime fails 13 of the new suite's cases.

Each breaking change is the Specification's or ADR-003's, so the alternative was not real; the flag records that a careful engineer would have told consumers first.

options.label: draft, provisional

experiments.question: Which v0.15.1 changes to bus-api are breaking (does a runtime that passes every v1 suite fail them); does a v2 stand-in pass the new suite, topology-dsl@v2's live suite and the other suites; which consumer cases break; do the new cases pin each clause; how does start() settle a writer before its readers; which Dart functions compare == across evaluations?
experiments.finding: New suite (108 cases, 42 guarantees, structure clean, S17 prototype 0 problems): v2 runtime 108/108; v1 runtime (topology-dsl-write-chain's write-chain runtime) 95/108, the 13 failures being exactly the cases of the four breaking changes (G9, G25, four G34 for the barrier; two G42; two G18 and two G41; one G23); minimal barrier 96/108, its settled-writer trace showing bus.y:0 and bus.z:0 before the settled values. v1 suite on v2: 76/98 (22 cases reversed or activating MODULE before start()). Live suite 49/49 on v2 and v1. Other suites on v2: bus-testing@v1 39/47, navigation-api@v1 41/41 and 52/52, flutter-binding@v1 55/57 and 26/26; all pass on v1. Probe P2: only v2 gives a reader activated before its writer the settled value as its first emission, within start(). Probe P1: top-level, static, const-receiver and const callable tear-offs compare == across evaluations; closures and tear-offs on new receivers (even with ==) do not. Eleven seeded defects each fail the cases of the clause they break.
